Thanks for this newfound archive!

As Adam mentioned, the spoken word intros are really special to discover and preserve. They put context and character behind otherwise ordinary lines of code. I am not sure how common this practice was for cassette releases in the 70s-80s but I’ve certainly enjoyed the ones preserved for Bally (the spoken narration for O’Jello is also detailed in Astrocast #7).

You also remind us of how many unheard of programs may still be floating around on dusty and forgotten cassettes, from individuals who may have developed programs but never formerly distributed them or only within small circles. This reminds me of a personal preservation effort for the Mattel Aquarius earlier this year. Someone had acquired an Aquarius that included a home data cassette from 1986 called House of Terrors. On it was an incredibly well developed machine language game that would’ve given any commercial title a run for its money had it been released. Not one person in the history of collecting and indexing every artifact for Aquarius had known about it until that very moment, 35 years after it was developed. The user didn’t have the means to do a faithful digitization, but through guidance was able to capture the sound through their phone and upload the video. From that, I was able to clean it up and produce a perfect running copy, which I then converted to both CAQ and clean digital WAV formats that could then be enjoyed on emulation and the actual device. It was really an incredible find and to manage preservation in such a round-about manner was excellent. The developer actually joined the small Aquarius community afterward and noted how he had developed a few games for the platform, I recall he said he distributed them scarcely at small local trade shows or events. He had developed at least two others but sadly has no copies. There have been other times people had rare and undigitized games for that platform but by the time they tried to record and upload the data the tapes had corroded beyond repair…

I appreciate your comprehensive preservation efforts.

Matt

I've archived Tic Tac Toe by E. Schoo. Thanks to Allen Schweitzer for loaning me this tape. This program seems to be completely unknown, and a quick search didn't reveal anything about the programmer. This is a reminder that for all the programs published or advertised in a newsletter, there were probably many more that people just experimented with on their own.

https://archive.org/details/tic-tac-toe-e-schoo
Tic Tac Toe by E. Schoo for the Astrocade console in 2000 baud format, load with:

:INPUT; RUN

So far as I can tell, this program was never published. The tape was included with an eBay purchase, but no further details of the source are known. The front side of the tape includes audio instructions and a copy of the program with a title screen. The reverse side of the tape includes an extra copy of the program, which seems to differ only in that it doesn't have a title screen. I digitally processed the programs with ballybin after applying a bandpass filter.

Paul
18640:
It only required the common 16K memory expansion cartridge and mini-expander
(joysticks). It is loaded in the same manner as most machine language
cassette games that were released commercially at the time, where you first
load a small BASIC loader program, then run that and play the cassette again
to load the actual machine language data that gets put into memory. All of
the visuals are just using the standard character set but done creatively,
it's the only game that has the 'running man' that can actually duck!

You can see the Aquarius II at 12:25 of this video and a close-up a little
later: https://youtu.be/dhpxhPtscpg?t=745 - From a recent retro computer
festival. It was a fully functional system and did get a very limited
release including full packaging and a written manual, but they scrapped a
lot of the plans for it including a planned high-resolution customizable
graphic mode and more internal RAM. It was essentially just an Aquarius I
with the Extended BASIC cart built into ROM, but with a much more usable
keyboard.

Matt

----------------------------------------

Tic Tac Toe
By E. Schoo
198x.


This game is for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade and AstroBASIC.

----------

The transcription of the game's instructions were made from the audio instructions that preceded the game on the tape.  The transcription was made by Adam Trionfo on December 7, 2021.  The text has not been changed, although punctuation has been added to make the instructions easier to read.

----------

The game that is on this tape now is Tac-Tac-Toe.  You input the number of games that you wish to play on the keyboard.  It is designed for two players.  Number one player starts, selects number with knob, pulls trigger when desired number is shown.  The machine will show that number with a question mark.  If you do not wish that number, push knob away from body and you can turn a new number with the knob.  If you wish to use the number, then pull trigger and X will be put in the square you selected.  Number two player does the same thing.

When the game is tied, a new game will be displayed.

The computer is programmed not to accept a number other than those of your coordinates.  Also, if a number has been used previously, it will not accept the number again.  When this occurs, the trigger will not accept it.  It will bring back the number so you may select a new one on your time.

Good luck, and load the tape at the BEEP tone.

=================================

The archive thread for this game is here:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/archived_tic_tac_toe_by_e/87557251

---------------------------------------- 

From: Michael Matte
Sent: Thursday, December 9, 2021

Bye.
MCM

Running across the OpenCorporates website inspired me to look up Astrocade, Inc. Here's the main company, incorporated in Delaware (common for tax purposes):

https://opencorporates.com/companies/us_de/895260

They were legally incorporated July 3, 1980. Delaware doesn't offer much free info on-line, but you can find what there is by looking up File Number 895260 here:

https://icis.corp.delaware.gov/Ecorp/EntitySearch/NameSearch.aspx

You can pay $20 for the tax assessment and filing history, but apparently that doesn't give you the documents themselves, which you'd need to call to order.

They also registered a branch in California on May 13, 1982:

https://opencorporates.com/companies/us_ca/C1111453

California's records are here:

https://businesssearch.sos.ca.gov/CBS/SearchResults?SearchType=NUMBER&SearchCriteria=C1111453

They actually let you see the registration document for free:

https://businesssearch.sos.ca.gov/Document/RetrievePDF?Id=01111453-3459400

OpenCorporates lists a May 1, 1984, "FTFT" filing for the branch, but I have no idea what this is or what their source is for it:

https://opencorporates.com/filings/899565005

Did anyone play this educational game when they were younger against a friend of family member?

Running across the OpenCorporates website inspired me to look up Astrocade, Inc. Here's the main company, incorporated in Delaware (common for tax purposes):

https://opencorporates.com/companies/us_de/895260

They were legally incorporated July 3, 1980. Delaware doesn't offer much free info on-line, but you can find what there is by looking up File Number 895260 here:

https://icis.corp.delaware.gov/Ecorp/EntitySearch/NameSearch.aspx

You can pay $20 for the tax assessment and filing history, but apparently that doesn't give you the documents themselves, which you'd need to call to order.

They also registered a branch in California on May 13, 1982:

https://opencorporates.com/companies/us_ca/C1111453

California's records are here:

https://businesssearch.sos.ca.gov/CBS/SearchResults?SearchType=NUMBER&SearchCriteria=C1111453

They actually let you see the registration document for free:

https://businesssearch.sos.ca.gov/Document/RetrievePDF?Id=01111453-3459400

OpenCorporates lists a May 1, 1984, "FTFT" filing for the branch, but I have no idea what this is or what their source is for it:

https://opencorporates.com/filings/899565005

Paul

It's been quite some time since any new Astrocade tapes have showed up, but I was recently loaned two rare commercial tapes I hadn't seen before--Tiny Arcade's Tape 103 and A.R.D.'s Gamepack G1. They're both from 1982 and for AstroBASIC. I was able to successfully archive all the recordings--9 unique programs, two with a duplicate copy. This includes 4 never before archived programs--Vindicator (Tiny Arcade), Art Show (Tiny Arcade), Caterpillar (A.R.D.), and Galactic Hitchhiker (A.R.D.). It's odd to think that I'm quite likely the first person to play these in 30+ years. Thanks to Alan Schweitzer for tracking these down and to Athena for loaning them out.

Here are some notes on my experience. I'll award best game to Caterpillar, and worst game to Galactic Hitchhiker.


Tiny Arcade Tape 103

Vindicator side: Two copies on tape, no apparent differences, but not byte for byte identical. No title screen. It's a space shooter that looks a bit like Defender. Your ship automatically moves from left to right before wrapping back to the left side of the screen. You can push left or right to slow down or speed up. Push up or down to move up or down. Pull the trigger to fire a beam a short distance in front of your ship. Use the beam to take out five stationary targets, which can fire horizontally in either direction. Avoid rockets moving directly up from the ground. Once you take out all the targets, more will generate. You have five lives to score as many points as possible. I found the rockets frustrating, as they respawn once they hit you or move above your ship, so you can get hit repeatedly when trying to take out targets near the ground.

Fireworks/Art Show side.
First recording is Fireworks. No title screen. Runs automatically.
Second recording is Art Show. Enter option 1-7 to decide what to see.
[1] Computer Crochet
[2] Spirathon
[3] Jewel Box
[4] Radiation
[5] Tones I
[6] Starflakes
[7] Combined Display


Gamepack G1 has five recordings on the front.
Part 1: Micro-Pac
This is a very slow Pac-Man clone where the ghosts can pass through walls. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 2: Caterpillar
The raw recording jumps at one point. I couldn't get the first recording to process correctly, but the second recording worked with the -l2 option. It's a Centipede clone. Move left and right with the joystick and pull the trigger to shoot at the caterpillar and occasional spiders. You only fire when lined up with the spider or the head of the caterpillar. There's no up or down motion, so you lose a life if the caterpillar or spider reaches the bottom of the screen. The speed is good for BASIC, but it gets difficult to see the caterpillar through the background mushrooms as the game progresses.
Part 3: Tic-Tac-Tollah
Enter moves with keypad. Invalid entries crash program. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 4: The Paper Chase
Grab the highlighted toilet paper roll by turning the knob to aim and pulling the trigger. You compete against a computer controlled opponent. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 5: Galactic Hitchhiker
I found it difficult to figure out how to play this, an opinion shared by the review in Arcadian volume 5, issue 3. I think you use the joystick to steer around obstacles rushing toward you in a first person view. But I'm not sure what you're supposed to do when it tells you to avoid rays.

Gamepack G1 had one recording on the reverse side, which is a copy of Micro-Pac. It works fine but has extraneous text on the title screen.

Paul

It's been quite some time since any new Astrocade tapes have showed up, but I was recently loaned two rare commercial tapes I hadn't seen before--Tiny Arcade's Tape 103 and A.R.D.'s Gamepack G1. They're both from 1982 and for AstroBASIC. I was able to successfully archive all the recordings--9 unique programs, two with a duplicate copy. This includes 4 never before archived programs--Vindicator (Tiny Arcade), Art Show (Tiny Arcade), Caterpillar (A.R.D.), and Galactic Hitchhiker (A.R.D.). It's odd to think that I'm quite likely the first person to play these in 30+ years. Thanks to Alan Schweitzer for tracking these down and to Athena for loaning them out.

Here are some notes on my experience. I'll award best game to Caterpillar, and worst game to Galactic Hitchhiker.


Tiny Arcade Tape 103

Vindicator side: Two copies on tape, no apparent differences, but not byte for byte identical. No title screen. It's a space shooter that looks a bit like Defender. Your ship automatically moves from left to right before wrapping back to the left side of the screen. You can push left or right to slow down or speed up. Push up or down to move up or down. Pull the trigger to fire a beam a short distance in front of your ship. Use the beam to take out five stationary targets, which can fire horizontally in either direction. Avoid rockets moving directly up from the ground. Once you take out all the targets, more will generate. You have five lives to score as many points as possible. I found the rockets frustrating, as they respawn once they hit you or move above your ship, so you can get hit repeatedly when trying to take out targets near the ground.

Fireworks/Art Show side.
First recording is Fireworks. No title screen. Runs automatically.
Second recording is Art Show. Enter option 1-7 to decide what to see.
[1] Computer Crochet
[2] Spirathon
[3] Jewel Box
[4] Radiation
[5] Tones I
[6] Starflakes
[7] Combined Display


Gamepack G1 has five recordings on the front.
Part 1: Micro-Pac
This is a very slow Pac-Man clone where the ghosts can pass through walls. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 2: Caterpillar
The raw recording jumps at one point. I couldn't get the first recording to process correctly, but the second recording worked with the -l2 option. It's a Centipede clone. Move left and right with the joystick and pull the trigger to shoot at the caterpillar and occasional spiders. You only fire when lined up with the spider or the head of the caterpillar. There's no up or down motion, so you lose a life if the caterpillar or spider reaches the bottom of the screen. The speed is good for BASIC, but it gets difficult to see the caterpillar through the background mushrooms as the game progresses.
Part 3: Tic-Tac-Tollah
Enter moves with keypad. Invalid entries crash program. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 4: The Paper Chase
Grab the highlighted toilet paper roll by turning the knob to aim and pulling the trigger. You compete against a computer controlled opponent. Seems the same as the copy we had before.
Part 5: Galactic Hitchhiker
I found it difficult to figure out how to play this, an opinion shared by the review in Arcadian volume 5, issue 3. I think you use the joystick to steer around obstacles rushing toward you in a first person view. But I'm not sure what you're supposed to do when it tells you to avoid rays.

Gamepack G1 had one recording on the reverse side, which is a copy of Micro-Pac. It works fine but has extraneous text on the title screen.

Paul

18695:
Michael Matte has been steadily working on his Hi-Res Astrocade project.  He has tracked down the intermittent trouble that he was having with hi-res screen RAM writes.  Here is the update the he sent to me two days ago.

----------------------------------------

From: Michael Matte
Sent: Wednesday, December 15, 2021 8:08 PM
To: Adam Trionfo
Subject: Progress Report

Progress Report
MCMs Final Hi-Res Astrocade
Dec 2021

Good news. The TV display disturbance issue I mentioned to you in my previous email has been resolved. My project breadboard 1 now runs perfect in low and hi-res. Yippy!

The disturbance was not generated by a noisy signal line, but by some active low CAS lines (screen RAM chip selects) that were not remaining at logic 0 long enough to finish their intended purpose. A simple rewire fixed the problem. The hard part was to find the bug, which took hours to find.

My early observation of running hi-res programs was suggesting a problem with reading screen RAM, but not writing to it. The TV disturbance did not occur in every hi-res program which would read screen RAM. This inconsistency was hard to diagnose.

I checked the TV display scan scheme and some other things on the breadboard to see if the bug was there. Then I was really focusing on the four 74LS245 enable (on/off) pins because those chips were turning on and off a lot during a hi-res program. Not knowing any better, I thought this frequent switching might be creating a TV disturbance because the 4 screen RAM data buses were also connected to the TV display scan scheme. Running out of things to test, I was actually looking to do some kind of rewire to keep those 4 chips from turning on and off so much.
Then a thought popped into my head that I might be risking a failure of this motherboard custom data chip because I was doing a lot of experimenting (rewiring) relating to the operation of the screen RAM data buses, so I decided to swap the data chip with a data chip I had that ran great in low or hi-res BUT displayed odd colors. Better to have this odd chip fail than my other perfect running data chip.

I installed this odd data chip and noticed a big reduction in the TV disturbances, but now the low and hi-res programs were crashing. At this point, I was getting really aggravated at this whole scenario. What's going on here?

A little later, a thought popped into my head. Today, I am still wondering if this thought came from above. This is not the first time I've experienced "out of nowhere" thoughts. The thought was that the 4 CAS_ signal lines (chip selects) for the 4 screen SRAM chips may not be remaining active low long enough to complete successfully all data reads from the Z80 CPU or all reads during the TV display scan scheme and there was an easy rewire to extend this active low signal another say 8nS.

I just happen to have a spare "AND" gate on the breadboard. I wired it in where it needed to be. I powered on my project set up. There were NO more crashes and NO TV disturbances. What? Are you kidding me?

I swapped data chips again. Now the perfect running data chip was installed. I powered on the project set up, ran the hi-res programs where the TV display disturbances were occurring. There were now NO disturbances of any kind. I ran into my living room jumping/speaking with joy. I found the bug. The hi-res issue is gone.

I ran the hi-res programs for a long time. This breadboard now runs great in low and hi-res.

My guess is that apparently the read operation for the CAS_signal lines was occurring at the very end of its active low cycle and creating some read issues in the TV display scan resulting in some TV display disturbances.

I previously had 2 other issues, one which was a Z80 screen RAM read issue. I created a simpler, more accurate Dwg 4 decoder/filter scheme because my logic analyzer revealed an undesirable "logic 0 down tick" using the original Dwg 4 scheme. This new scheme fixed the Z80 read issue.

Digital integrated circuits (chips) of the same type have operating output tolerances. The outputs of the same type chips do not perform identically. I'm hoping that my revised low/hi-res screen SRAM scheme is now tweaked so it will be compatible with any Astrocade motherboard. I would like to try my revised scheme on 2 other motherboards, but I will have to wait until my revised scheme is officially wire wrapped on a prototype board.

I plan to record a video progress report for my YouTube channel with me playing around with my project board set up. You saw this setup in a previous video. This time I will be running the project board with low and hi-res graphic programs. That will be fun capturing on video this completed, perfect running project breadboard 1. This new video should be available for viewing in a few days.

Bye.
MCM

----------------------------------------

I adore reading Michael's down-to-earth explanations of of his Astrocade projects.

Of course, you can read the complete Hi-Res thread on AtariAge, here:

https://atariage.com/forums/topic/254592-hi-res-bally-arcadeastrocade-correspondence/?do=findComment&comment=4968025

I hope that someday there will be a few people who follow Michael's lead and upgrade their Astrocade systems to use hi-res mode.  Heck, maybe someone might poke around in a similar area and program one of the Bally Arcade games that use the Bally custom chips (i.e. Wizard of Wor, Gorf, among others) to play around in the high-res sandbox.

Adam

----------------------------------------

From: Michael Matte
Sent: Wednesday, December 15, 2021 8:08 PM
To: Adam Trionfo
Subject: Progress Report
 
Progress Report
MCMs Final Hi-Res Astrocade
Dec 2021

Good news. The TV display disturbance issue I mentioned to you in my previous email has been resolved. My project breadboard 1 now runs perfect in low and hi-res. Yippy!

The disturbance was not generated by a noisy signal line, but by some active low CAS lines (screen RAM chip selects) that were not remaining at logic 0 long enough to finish their intended purpose. A simple rewire fixed the problem. The hard part was to find the bug, which took hours to find.

My early observation of running hi-res programs was suggesting a problem with reading screen RAM, but not writing to it. The TV disturbance did not occur in every hi-res program which would read screen RAM. This inconsistency was hard to diagnose.

I checked the TV display scan scheme and some other things on the breadboard to see if the bug was there. Then I was really focusing on the four 74LS245 enable (on/off) pins because those chips were turning on and off a lot during a hi-res program. Not knowing any better, I thought this frequent switching might be creating a TV disturbance because the 4 screen RAM data buses were also connected to the TV display scan scheme. Running out of things to test, I was actually looking to do some kind of rewire to keep those 4 chips from turning on and off so much.
Then a thought popped into my head that I might be risking a failure of this motherboard custom data chip because I was doing a lot of experimenting (rewiring) relating to the operation of the screen RAM data buses, so I decided to swap the data chip with a data chip I had that ran great in low or hi-res BUT displayed odd colors. Better to have this odd chip fail than my other perfect running data chip.

I installed this odd data chip and noticed a big reduction in the TV disturbances, but now the low and hi-res programs were crashing. At this point, I was getting really aggravated at this whole scenario. What's going on here?

A little later, a thought popped into my head. Today, I am still wondering if this thought came from above. This is not the first time I've experienced "out of nowhere" thoughts. The thought was that the 4 CAS_ signal lines (chip selects) for the 4 screen SRAM chips may not be remaining active low long enough to complete successfully all data reads from the Z80 CPU or all reads during the TV display scan scheme and there was an easy rewire to extend this active low signal another say 8nS.

I just happen to have a spare "AND" gate on the breadboard. I wired it in where it needed to be. I powered on my project set up. There were NO more crashes and NO TV disturbances. What? Are you kidding me?

I swapped data chips again. Now the perfect running data chip was installed. I powered on the project set up, ran the hi-res programs where the TV display disturbances were occurring. There were now NO disturbances of any kind. I ran into my living room jumping/speaking with joy. I found the bug. The hi-res issue is gone.

I ran the hi-res programs for a long time. This breadboard now runs great in low and hi-res.

My guess is that apparently the read operation for the CAS_signal lines was occurring at the very end of its active low cycle and creating some read issues in the TV display scan resulting in some TV display disturbances.

I previously had 2 other issues, one which was a Z80 screen RAM read issue. I created a simpler, more accurate Dwg 4 decoder/filter scheme because my logic analyzer revealed an undesirable "logic 0 down tick" using the original Dwg 4 scheme. This new scheme fixed the Z80 read issue.

Digital integrated circuits (chips) of the same type have operating output tolerances. The outputs of the same type chips do not perform identically. I'm hoping that my revised low/hi-res screen SRAM scheme is now tweaked so it will be compatible with any Astrocade motherboard. I would like to try my revised scheme on 2 other motherboards, but I will have to wait until my revised scheme is officially wire wrapped on a prototype board.

I plan to record a video progress report for my YouTube channel with me playing around with my project board set up. You saw this setup in a previous video. This time I will be running the project board with low and hi-res graphic programs. That will be fun capturing on video this completed, perfect running project breadboard 1. This new video should be available for viewing in a few days.

Bye.
MCM

18709:
If we're gonna have a Blue Ram compatible device at all, then it should be 100% compatible.  Else, the Lil' White Ram (LWR) probably does all that most people need.  Here are some reasons I like the Blue Ram and use it:

1) Blue Ram BASIC (BRB) - Many programs require this BASIC.  The Lil' White Ram doesn't work with it.  If you're writing new Extended BASIC software, then that's okay, as ViperSoft BASIC does pretty-much everything BRB does and it works with the LWR.  However, most of the expansion BASIC software was made for BRB.

2) Blue Ram Utility - I may be the only person who uses this utility software, but it's useful to me for various archiving tools.  Ken Lill changed the code to make it work with the LWR and renamed it--- White Ram Utility (or something like that).  I've not actually used this modified version.  Has anyone else here used it?

I agree with Ken, these features of the Blue Ram are NOT required:

1) Compatibility with the 300 BAUD modem - OLD
2) Compatibility with BSR Controller - OLD.  I bet most people don't even know what the means.

Some hardware features of the Blue Ram that I like, but don't really use are:

1) Serial Port - Printers and keyboard
2) Parallel Port - Printers and... what else?

The Blue Ram keyboard option is nice, but it requires Blue RAM BASIC or a keyboard driver for AstroBASIC, which uses many of those previous 1,800 bytes of RAM.

I made a video review of the Blue Ram hardware about three years ago:

Having said all of this, I like my Lil' White Ram, but I'm glad that I have the Blue Ram expansion too.

Ths Blue RAM circuitry has several things that I feel aren't really needed here. There is a 2K/6K switch already on the LWR. There is an AUTO-RAM-ROM switch which is basically on the LWR, it just doesn't have the AUTO feature. An then there's the 2 pin ZIF socket. The ONLY thing we might want to keep that is far a Blue RAM type keyboard. The other features that Perkins Engineering used it for (300 baud modem and BSR controller) are obsolete things of the 80's. That's around 40 year old technology.

A Blue RAM will cost somewhere in the neighborhood of $200. The add in may be around $100.

MAME doesn't support "hot" cartridge swapping, so these games and programs can only be used on real Bally Arcade/Astrocade hardware. Yesterday I studied this issue more closely, read the documentation and came to the following conclusions:

1. You can't just take the binary code from the digital cassette images created with BallyBin and load it as a cartridge. Well, at least this applies to programs in BASIC - they need an interpreter.
2. On the other hand, after examining the Bally Astrocade memory map, I concluded that it is technically feasible. BASIC takes up only half of the available space of the cartridge, so the remaining 4 kilobytes will fit both the BASIC code, the bootloader, and even a small splash screen. Naturally, BASIC will need to be slightly modified so that it immediately launches the program. I see possible difficulties associated with addressing, but the BASIC code can be copied into RAM and run from there. If no one has done this en masse before, then there are still some pitfalls that I do not know about. I'm talking about BallyBasic, because Blue Ram Basic and ViperBasic occupy all 8 kb of space.
3. There is another way for real Jedi - to write a BASIC compiler that translates the program into machine code. But this is a very time consuming path.

Kevin beat me to this answer; yes, it's possible to "autoboot" a BASIC cartridge.  This topic has come up on numerous times in this forum in the last twenty years (!) or so.  I guess a search would turn up some information, but a cookbook process to create a BASICart has never been created (yet?).  If anyone can find links to useful BASICart posts made in the last two decades, then posting them to this thread would be extremely helpful.

The "Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ" has some useful getting-started information if you want to learn about the history and uses of BASICarts.  This FAQ is pretty long, so search for the term "BASICart" in it:

https://ballyalley.com/faqs/astrocade_cart_and_hardware_faq.txt

Michael White, who made many of these BASICarts in about 1986, made the
"BASICart Code Key" for his self-reference for when he was creating a BASICart.  It can be downloaded here, although it's pretty cryptic:

https://ballyalley.com/basic/BASICart_Code_Key.pdf

I've never made a BASICart, although one member of this group, Ken Lill, has some experience with this method.  Richard Degler also has made a few of these "autoboot" cartridges, but he passed away a couple of years ago.

One of the earliest cartridges ever made for the Bally Arcade was released in 1978.  It is the "BASIC Demo Cart."  It uses this "autoboot" method to load the example programs.  You can watch this demo running here:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pGlqIZfnB3M
[https://i.ytimg.com/vi/pGlqIZfnB3M/hqdefault.jpg]<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pGlqIZfnB3M>
Bally Arcade / Astrocade - Bally BASIC Demo (1978) - YouTube<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pGlqIZfnB3M>
Bally BASIC Demo, by Bally Mfg. Corp. - Functional Series - 8K cart - 1978.This cartridge has a small (about 6") chain attached to the top-front. This cartri...
www.youtube.com
I wrote a short article about this program about twenty years ago:

https://ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/basic_demo_cart.txt

Here is a printout of the Bally BASIC program that is contained in the Bally BASIC Demo cartridge:

https://ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/bally_basic_demo_cart.pdf

If I recall, this program is about 3.5K, which breaks the 1.8K Bally BASIC memory limit.  I forget how this trick works.

There are two reasons that non-bootable BASIC cartridges exist:

1) Two programs can be fit on an 8K cartridge instead of one.

2) AstroBASIC doesn't have to be distributed with these homemade carts.  In around 1985 when this BASIC cart method was first used in the Astrocade community, I think that this was still a legal issue.

The BASICarts already contains the 4K version of AstroBASIC that has been modified to make a BASICart.  Hopefull Ken Lill jumps into this conversation with some hints for us all about creating a BASICart from scratch.

Adam

18743:
The cartridge-based games you mention are machine language developed (Z80 assembly code), which opens up a world of enhanced capabilities including the number of colors on the screen, sprite and draw control, framerate and so on. Even extended basic with extra RAM can’t really compensate for those limitations, and since BASIC is always an interpreted language it will be magnitudes slower than directly communicating with the ICs.

 

Matt
